strengths: Introduces VisJudge-Bench, apparently the first large-scale benchmark (3,090 expert-annotated samples across 32 chart types, single/multi-vis/dashboard) specifically targeting visualization aesthetics and quality assessment, filling a clear gap between generic image-aesthetics benchmarks and chart-QA/NL2VIS benchmarks.

The 'Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics' framework, decomposed into six measurable sub-dimensions with adaptive, chart-specific question/rubric generation, is a thoughtful and well-motivated evaluation design grounded in visualization theory (Tufte, Cleveland & McGill, Munzner).

Extensive experimental evaluation across seven strong, up-to-date MLLMs including GPT-5, Claude-4/3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.0/2.5, and Qwen2.5-VL, with detailed per-dimension MAE/MSE/correlation analysis, bias/distribution analysis, and complexity-stratified (single/multi/dashboard) breakdowns.

Proposes VisJudge, a GRPO-fine-tuned specialized model that meaningfully improves MAE and correlation over all tested baselines including GPT-5, along with qualitative case studies illustrating specific failure modes (score inflation, overly conservative bias) that are corrected by fine-tuning.

Very thorough appendix documenting data collection/filtering pipeline, annotator recruitment and quality-control mechanisms, full evaluation rubrics/prompt templates for every dimension and visualization type, and multiple categories of case studies, which supports transparency and potential reproducibility.
weaknesses: No inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha, Fleiss' kappa) are reported despite using three independent crowd annotators plus expert adjudication; given inherently subjective aesthetic dimensions, this is an important omission for validating the 'gold standard' ground truth.

The dataset construction pipeline relies heavily on GPT-4o for filtering, classification, metadata extraction, and adaptive question generation, which is later itself evaluated as one of the baseline models (GPT-4o), raising potential circularity/contamination concerns for the benchmark's fairness.

Scaling law claims (Section 5.2.5) are drawn from a narrow range (0–2,442 training samples) with single-epoch runs and are presented as 'predictable' with high R² despite the small number of data points; the strength of this claim seems overstated.

Absolute performance of VisJudge itself remains modest (overall correlation 0.681, many individual sub-dimensions still below 0.6), yet the paper's language ('near-perfect alignment,' 'significant improvement') arguably overstates how well the gap with human experts has actually been closed.

No ablations isolating the contribution of GRPO vs. simpler supervised fine-tuning, no comparison against other open-source base models or fine-tuning recipes, and no test of VisJudge's generalization to visualization types/domains outside the training distribution (train/test split is drawn from the same stratified pool).

Ethical and copyright considerations around web-crawled visualization images (many likely copyrighted business/analytics screenshots) are only briefly addressed in the ethics statement, without clear discussion of licensing or opt-out mechanisms.
The 'rationale' text generated by VisJudge is only assessed qualitatively via a handful of case studies rather than through systematic human evaluation of reasoning quality/faithfulness.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified gap: no existing benchmark systematically evaluates MLLMs as judges of visualization quality along fidelity, expressiveness, and aesthetics simultaneously, distinguishing this work from chart-QA benchmarks (ChartQA, ChartInsights) and general image-aesthetics benchmarks (AVA, ArtiMuse).

Large-scale, diverse benchmark (3,090 samples spanning 32 chart subtypes across single visualizations, multi-view visualizations, and dashboards) with a well-documented three-stage data pipeline (crawling, MLLM-assisted filtering/classification, stratified sampling).

Rigorous-looking annotation protocol: strict annotator screening, validation-check items to catch careless workers, a systematic disagreement-resolution mechanism (outlier removal, malicious-scoring detection, sub-dimension bias correction), and final expert adjudication, all described in detail in the appendix.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation of 7 representative MLLMs (including GPT-5) revealing consistent and interpretable findings: hierarchical capability differences across Fidelity/Expressiveness/Aesthetics, systematic score-inflation and over-conservative biases, and performance degradation with visualization complexity (single < multi < dashboard).

The proposed VisJudge model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B + LoRA + GRPO with a well-specified composite reward) shows a clear, sizable improvement over all baselines (19.8% MAE reduction, 58.7% correlation improvement vs. GPT-5), together with a scaling-law analysis of training data size.

Extensive appendix with case studies (high/medium/low score, dimension-specific, and per-model error analyses), full evaluation prompts/rubrics, and training/hyperparameter details, supporting reproducibility and giving qualitative insight into failure modes.
weaknesses: Even after specialized fine-tuning, VisJudge's correlation with human scores is only 0.681 (and much lower per-dimension, e.g., ~0.5-0.6 for aesthetics sub-dimensions), which is still a fairly modest agreement level; the paper's framing ("near-perfect alignment") mainly refers to matching the mean of the score distribution rather than point-wise agreement, which could overstate the practical reliability of the judge.

No inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha, ICC) are reported for the crowd-sourced or expert-validated scores, making it hard to assess the intrinsic reliability ceiling of the benchmark, especially for the highly subjective Aesthetics dimension where all models (and presumably annotators) show the weakest correlations.

The benchmark construction pipeline (filtering, classification, chart-metadata extraction, and adaptive question generation) itself heavily relies on GPT-4o, and GPT-4o/Claude models are also among the evaluated judges; this creates a potential circularity/self-selection bias where content and question templates may be systematically easier or harder for models used in construction.

VisJudge is trained and tested on splits of the same benchmark; no cross-benchmark or out-of-distribution generalization experiment is provided to show the fine-tuned judge generalizes beyond VisJudge-Bench's specific annotation style and question templates.

No comparison against non-MLLM baselines (e.g., rule-based or learning-based visualization quality/recommendation methods such as Draco, VizML, ColInsight mentioned in related work) or simpler prompting/ensembling baselines, limiting the picture of how much value the specialized fine-tuning adds relative to cheaper alternatives.

Statistical significance of the reported improvements (MAE/correlation differences across models, only 648 test samples, 3 runs) is not tested, so it is unclear whether some of the finer-grained comparisons (e.g., between closely performing commercial models) are robust.

The annotator pool, while requiring a Bachelor's degree and relevant occupational background, are recruited via a general crowdsourcing platform (CloudResearch) rather than domain experts in data visualization design, which somewhat qualifies the paper's repeated characterization of the ground truth as "expert-annotated".

strengths: Introduces VisJudge-Bench, a large-scale (3,090 samples, 32 chart subtypes across single visualizations, multi-visualizations, and dashboards) and, to the authors' knowledge, first comprehensive benchmark for MLLM-based visualization aesthetics/quality assessment, addressing a clear gap relative to chart-QA, natural-image aesthetics, and NL2VIS benchmarks.

The 'Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics' framework is well-motivated by classical visualization/design theory and operationalized into six measurable sub-dimensions with adaptive, chart-specific rewritten scoring rubrics rather than generic criteria.

Rigorous, well-documented three-stage annotation pipeline (603 screened crowdworkers, validation checks, statistical disagreement detection, and expert adjudication) with substantial appendix detail on quality control, annotator demographics, and quality-control impact analysis, supporting reproducibility.

Extensive empirical evaluation of 12 representative MLLMs (including GPT-5, Claude-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro) across multiple metrics (MAE, MSE, Pearson correlation), sub-dimensions, and visualization complexity levels, plus systematic bias analysis (score inflation vs. conservatism) supported by concrete case studies.

The proposed VisJudge model (GRPO fine-tuning with composite reward) shows consistent, sizeable improvements over baselines across four different open-source backbones (3B–8B, different architectures), suggesting the training approach is not overfit to one architecture.

Additional generalization experiments integrating VisJudge into real downstream systems (MatPlotAgent for generation, HAIChart for recommendation) under distribution shift provide some evidence of practical utility beyond the benchmark itself.
Thorough training-scale analysis (Figure 8) characterizing how correlation and error scale with training data size, offering practical guidance on data efficiency.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest even after fine-tuning (best correlation 0.687, MAE 0.421), and crowd-crowd MAE (0.64–0.70) is not dramatically smaller than crowd-expert MAE (0.54–0.59), suggesting substantial inherent annotator disagreement/subjectivity that tempers claims of a reliable 'gold standard' and of models 'narrowing the gap to human judgment.'

The dataset construction pipeline relies heavily on GPT-4o for classification, filtering, metadata extraction, and question/rubric generation, which risks circularity: the same family of models used to build ground-truth generation scaffolding is later evaluated as a subject, and downstream extended experiments (e.g., MatPlotAgent scores) are also evaluated by GPT-4o, potentially inflating apparent benefits of VisJudge as feedback.

The 'expert' validation stage is described only briefly (three individuals 'with visualization analysis experience'); it is unclear whether these constitute genuine domain experts (e.g., published visualization researchers or professional designers) as opposed to more experienced crowd/contract annotators, which affects how much weight should be placed on the benchmark as a true expert-grounded standard.

No confidence intervals or significance tests accompany the many point-estimate comparisons (MAE/correlation differences across 12+ models, ablations, and generalization tables), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (e.g., +23.9% MAE reduction) are robust given inherent annotation noise.

Data fidelity is assessed purely via visual inspection without access to underlying raw data (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), which limits the rigor of the 'Fidelity' dimension, arguably the most objective of the three.

The core methodological contribution (GRPO fine-tuning with an accuracy+format reward for regression/rationale generation) is relatively standard within the MLLM-as-judge/reward-model literature; the paper's main novelty lies primarily in the benchmark and framework rather than in a technically new training method.

Comparisons of 'improvement' percentages sometimes mix different baselines across metrics (e.g., best MAE from GPT-5, best correlation from GPT-4o), which can make the headline improvement numbers appear more favorable than a consistent single-baseline comparison would show.

Case studies presented as qualitative evidence (Figures 6, 7, 22–26) are inherently selective/cherry-picked and cannot substitute for a systematic, quantitative error-mode analysis with statistical backing.
